cues.text: A short video can repeat every word correctly and still tell the wrong story.
The mistake is often not an invented sentence. It is the sentence left outside the cut.
Consider this invented editing example. A creator tries a new workflow on one practice recording.
Removing dead air cut a ten minute editing pass to six minutes.
But that result came from one practice session, not a controlled comparison.
The number is useful context, not a promise about how much time everyone will save.
Another trap is dropping a tiny word that carries most of the meaning.
Do not remove every pause from an interview. Some pauses let an important answer land.
Delete the first two words and the instruction now says the opposite.
A better editing workflow starts with the source, rather than a pile of generated claims.
First choose complete caption ranges. Keep every word inside the selected range in its original order.
Then inspect the sentence before and the sentence after the cut. Look for explanations and qualifications.
If the next sentence changes the claim, include it or choose a different clip.
Captions should use the new clip timeline. A clip starting two minutes into a recording still needs captions near zero.
Every exported caption should point back to its original source cue. Editors need a trace, not a confident guess.
A transcript fingerprint lets another editor check whether the supplied transcript has changed.
However, a matching fingerprint does not prove the transcript matches the audio or that its claims are true.
No lexical rule can guarantee that a cut preserves every nuance. Context checks are reminders, not a substitute for judgment.
A useful workflow ends with real files: a playable clip, synchronized captions, and an edit record another person can inspect.
Good automation removes repetitive work without removing responsibility. Shorter cuts should not require a different story.

review_policy: Restoring requires reattaching the original video and reviewing cuts again. No media or credentials are saved.
